beta_new: This is one of the two main routes on Cannon Mountain and is recommended only as an ascent route. It's best done in mid-to-late summer once snow has melted from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. The route starts at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to the ridge crest, then follows and traverses below the crest -- including a notorious 0.3-mile loose traverse below a band of towers that can't be climbed directly -- before a talus gully and short final scramble to the summit block.

moves.from: most parties descend via the standard Prusik Pass/Druid Plateau line instead of reversing it

beta_new: Cannon has no maintained trail. The most-documented approaches reach a common staging area near Druid Plateau (east of the summit) either from Stuart Lake Trailhead via the Mountaineer Creek valley and Cannon Creek basin (cross-country, brushy lower section with cliff bands), or from the Core Enchantment Zone via Prusik Pass after the longer Snow Lakes Trail approach. From Druid Plateau, parties contour/scramble to the base of the summit block and finish on class 2-3 friction slab and boulders. Snow and verglass can linger on shaded sections into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain.

Same start as Chitlins Con Carne, but goes straight up after the 3rd bolt into a hard slab crux (5.11b/c) — a step-up move with bolts positioned right at your face — then continues past bolts (5.11-) to chains.

From a basin camp roughly 6,800–7,100 ft below the peak, parties cross moderate snow/scree slopes toward the saddle between the north and middle summits, then follow the summit ridge (Class 2-3, with a couple of steep snow patches early season) to the non-technical middle summit (~8,590 ft). Reaching the true, slightly higher south summit requires a short, exposed technical step (unrated low 5th class / easy mixed moves) that most guided descriptions treat as the crux; many scramblers stop at the middle summit rather than commit to it. When the north side holds snow, parties commonly drop onto the east/southeast slopes below the summit ridge (this route) rather than fight the icier north ridge.

From the Phelps Creek Trailhead, follow the wide Phelps Creek Trail for about a quarter mile, then bear right and steeply uphill onto the narrower, unmaintained-feel Carne Mountain Trail (#1508). It climbs via moderate-to-steep switchbacks through forest and across an open talus slope for roughly 2.5-2.9 miles to a small alpine basin (~6,100 ft) with campsites and a stream. From there the trail continues to a low pass/junction with the Old Gib Trail around mile 3, then climbs to a saddle (~6,800 ft) with views of Mount Maude, Clark Mountain, and Glacier Peak, before a final quarter mile along the ridge to the 7,085 ft summit.

Class 4-low 5th alpine rock route up Cascade Peak own short, broken summit tower via the NW Chimney -- reached via the same CJ Couloir most parties use to approach neighboring Johannesburg Mountain East Ridge. Roughly 3 pitches (a loose, wide crux crack, the 5.8 chimney, then a short, very loose finish) on consistently loose, broken rock with essentially no fixed protection or rappel anchors. Expect real routefinding, not a clean traveled line.

Graded 5.8, the Northwest Chimney climbs three pitches of broken, loose rock - including an aesthetic but sparsely-protected chimney pitch - from the moat below the peak's northwest side to the summit. Loose rock can make the crux first pitch feel considerably harder than that grade (closer to 5.10), and no rappel anchors, pitons or summit register have been reported, which suggests the route sees very few ascents.

From the Eightmile Trail, cut cross-country up through an old burn zone, then continue up and left toward the gully between the S and SE ridges. The S/SE gully is wide and offers a 'choose your own adventure' character: the center/right line is mostly class 2, while the climbers-left side holds solid class 3-4 rock. The gully tops out at roughly 8,150 ft, about 360 vertical feet below the 8,501 ft top. This line cuts the standard 8-9 mile one-way West Ridge approach roughly in half.

The standard and easiest route on Cashmere Mountain. From Windy Pass the west ridge becomes the obvious line: descend to a saddle where the scrambling begins, then work through a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by roughly five main gaps, weaving from the north side of the ridge to the south and back, rarely following the crest exactly. Cairns mark parts of the route but route-finding is required. Rock is generally solid granite but loose in spots near the summit; snow or rime can turn the Class 3 terrain into harder Class 4 climbing in early season or after storms, and parties have roped up with slings/chocks for running belays in those conditions.

Castle Peak's standard ascent is a granite scramble featuring mostly Class 2 terrain with sections of easy Class 3. Rock quality is excellent and reminiscent of the Stuart Range. Route-finding is required in micro-terrain and sections are steep with krummholz. The peak can be approached from three main directions, all requiring significant approach commitment.

Distinct from the East Ridge Couloir/Southeast Ridge line, this route stays on the peak's south side. From a camp near 5,500 ft in Castle Creek Basin, ascend the wide gully on the south side to about 6,800 ft, then enter the northeast gully aiming for a notch around 7,400 ft. The final section crosses granite slabs, boulders and snow patches with a short scramble to the true summit.
A 5.7 trad route in The Castle's climbing area alongside the easy-5th-class Southeast Face; no detailed pitch-by-pitch description, approach specifics, or first-ascent history is on record.

moves.from: Likely approached the same way as the Southeast Face — via the Pinnacle Peak Trail from Reflection Lakes and a traverse across Pinnacle's south-face scree to the Castle-Pinnacle area.

beta_new: From the Pinnacle Saddle Trailhead at Reflection Lakes, hike the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the ~5,920-ft saddle between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak, then leave the trail and contour east across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus (roughly 6,000-6,200 ft) to the Castle-Pinnacle col. From the col, scramble onto Castle's south rib, make a short class-3 traverse onto the east flank, and follow the obvious crack-chimney system (easy 5th class; some parties call this the East Face Chimney Route) up and right to a notch beside a natural rock horn. A brief, exposed class 3-4 scramble along the summit crest leads to the true (northernmost) summit block. Many parties fix a handline or belay the chimney pitch and always rappel or downclimb it on the return.

Put up by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in 2003. It starts where the original Northeast Ridge route ends its first pitch. From there, traverse left and up through scary, unstable Class 4+ rock on a short pitch, aiming for a left-hand vertical crack in a left-facing corner identified by yellow-speckled rock with roofs above. The third pitch follows that crack and exits over its left side — the route's best pitch, rated 5.7/5.8 and well protected. Above, the rock eases and parties navigate upward through variations, with a short difficult left-leaning crack at 5.9+ before moderate terrain leads to the summit area. It carries a PG13 protection rating and would deserve a higher star rating were it not for the precarious second pitch.

The Northwest Couloir climbs to a chockstone in the upper gully; parties commonly rappel or downclimb past the chockstone. Some parties descend it back toward Peggy's Pond, but the standard descent from the summit is the Southwest Face. The couloir holds notably loose, fractured rock.

Pitch-by-pitch beta for this line is not available. It begins on Chair's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant on 4th-class to low-5th-class rock, with one short, steep mandatory rappel (~50 ft) getting off Bryant — the same rappel found on the closely related 'Tooth - Chair Traverse,' which covers the Bryant-to-Chair portion of this ridge system.

Rated 5.2 (PG13) over 3 pitches, 600 ft (182 m); about 400 ft of the route's pleasant climbing is 4th to easy 5th class, with the notable overhanging band rated 5.5. Protection is sparse in places, with runouts over 50 ft reported on the traverse pitch.

Reached via a short traverse from the Source Lake-Snow Lake divide, the North Face offers about four pitches of steep snow and ice climbing on generally moderate-angle terrain (50-65°) with one short crux step that can approach 80° (sometimes rock, 5.4-5.6, if thin on ice). Abundant natural/fixed protection and a short approach make it a popular introduction to Cascade ice climbing, though it backs up with parties on clear winter weekends. Note: a distinct, harder rock variation called 'North Face Direct' (5.9, 5 pitches) starts about 200m from the standard line and should not be confused with this route.

From the basin below Chair Peak's East Face, the route climbs a curving gully system on climber's right before trending up and left along the buttress crest to the summit. The technical crux in winter conditions is a short, steep ice bulge encountered partway up. It is commonly done in 4 pitches with a 60m rope, though many parties simul-climb sections or break it into 5-6 shorter pitches, especially in early-season snow. Short approach and moderate climbing make it very popular and prone to queues on clear winter weekends.

This is a 6-pitch, 1,000 ft (303 m), Grade II, 5.7 trad route reached via the East Face approach to 'Thumbtack Rock' before angling right over the ridge. It has a low average rating (2/5 stars) reflecting run-out climbing and poor rock quality in places.

First climbed by Ian Nicholson and Tino Villanueva in summer/fall 2022, this 5.9- (Grade II) route climbs 8 pitches (800 ft / 242 m total, including a summit scramble) of slab and steeper rock on the East Face, protected mostly by bolts (11-12 quickdraws recommended). The crux is a 70 ft, 5.9 pitch (P5); pitches 6-7 have notably looser rock.

Established by Pro Guiding Service founder Martin Volken (first documented ascent reported July 25, 2007), the route is graded Alpine Grade 2+ / 5.7. It starts up a narrow 220 ft couloir to the low point of the ridge just east of a distinct tower (2 pitches of 5.7 to the top of the gully), then follows the ridge crest to the summit over varying rock quality and exposure.

From a camp near Butterfly Butte in the Napeequa Valley, climbers travel through larch and pumice terrain, pass north of the crevassed Pilz Glacier, traverse granite slabs and tarns below Chalangin's north ridge, and gain the ridge via a scree gully around 8,000 ft before a final scramble over loose rock ("choss") to the summit. An alternate finish drops directly off Luahna Peak's west ridge to the Luahna-Chalangin col and climbs from there — reported as harder than expected, with some exposed but non-technical (Class 3) scrambling. A Forest Service description of this same trailhead/valley approach frames the target line as Chalangin's southeast ridge.

From a high camp in Chalangin Basin (~5,100 ft), climbers ascend the open south slope/southwest face of the peak, passing through a rocky cliff band around 5,500-6,500 ft (one or two 4th-class moves), then traverse snow slopes above the Pilz Glacier before a cramponed finish (accounts describe the final push variously as the south slope, southwest face, or southeast face depending on the exact line and year's snow coverage) to the summit. This is reported as the shortest-distance, least-elevation-gain of the three known approaches to Chalangin.

Climbs a line of seams up the middle of the steep main face: thin boulder climbing up a steep wall to a small overhang, then a few big moves on good holds before easier terrain and the anchors, which are shared with the adjacent Firearms.

The summit can be reached either by hiking the Chelan Butte Trail from a WDFW trailhead on the south side of the town of Chelan (via Iowa Ave, roughly 7.46 mi round trip with 2,500 ft gain) or by driving/walking Chelan Butte Road from the Millard St trailhead in the Lakeside community (4.5 mi one-way, paved for the first 1.2 mi then dirt/gravel). Both converge on the same summit-road system. A bench at the Elephant Head viewpoint offers a rest stop partway up. The route is fully exposed to sun with essentially no shade.

Rebel Yell is a well-established North Cascades classic featuring 7 pitches of alpine trad climbing (5.10 overall with the 5.10b crux on P5). The route climbs the clean east face via splitter cracks with varied techniques. All pitches are led on gear. Descent via 4 double-rope rappels on fixed anchors. Extra gear can be cached at base. Typically done as 2-day expedition.

Established in 1989, this is the second-best-known line on Chianti's east face and a quieter alternative to Rebel Yell at a full grade easier. It starts directly below the summit, following a long left-leaning ramp up into a left-facing corner and an off-width crack; three more pitches cross Rebel Yell and gain the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti, and a short pitch reaches the summit up the normal route. It is graded II 5.9 or III 5.9. Detail is thin: pitch lengths and total footage are not known, so this is a route for a party comfortable route-finding on an alpine face rather than following a topo.

moves.from: Approach ... logistics are identical to Rebel Yell - the same Early Winters Creek trail to Burgundy Col, the same drop and traverse beneath Burgundy Spire's east face
Descent logistics are identical to Rebel Yell ... a rappel-based descent

beta_new: First ascensionists Joe Hieb and Art Maki approached via moraine and ice to the eastern walls of the Wine Spires group, made a roughly 250-ft rappel off the west face into the notch between Chianti and Burgundy Spires, and found the north face held the only route to the top. Two leads of unstable rock presented the main difficulties, protected with seven pitons for aid/safety, and the final moves to the tiny summit required a shoulder-stand and flipping the rope over a rock flake.

From the Mineral Creek Trailhead, follow the Mineral Creek Trail and past the Park Lakes to the Pacific Crest Trail. Head north on the PCT along the west side of Chikamin Ridge, then leave the trail around 5,500 ft to climb southeast-facing slabs, heather benches, and a broadening gully onto the crest of Chikamin Ridge. Follow the ridge/gully system to the summit horn, finishing with a short, well-protected Class 3 chimney (about 10 ft) and roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling to the top. An alternate approach from Glacier Lake/Chikamin Lake (via Mineral Creek and a Spectacle Point saddle) reaches the same upper mountain from the east.

Chimney Peak has no maintained trail to its summit. Parties approach via the long East Fork Quinault River backpack to Enchanted Valley Chalet, then travel off-trail north/northeast into the basin below the peak's southwest side, gain the southwest ridge, and follow class 3 terrain to the summit. The peak's south side is defined by very steep, waterfall-streaked cliffs (~4,800 ft of relief above the valley in under a mile), so route-finding onto moderate ground on the SW ridge/gully system is the key to keeping the climb at class 3. A separate, harder objective — "The Chimney," a ~100-ft rock tower on the peak's west aspect — was first climbed in 1970 at class 5.3 and is not part of this standard scramble line.

Solid 5.6 climbing that rejoins the East Face route about halfway up. Instead of the standard route's loose rock, this variation deals with a moat, which parties cross by building a snow anchor with a picket and jumping the gap. Nine pitches in all, mostly fourth class with short easy fifth-class steps.

From the upper Chimney Glacier, cross the moat at the foot of the rock and climb the face to the left of the main gully that drops from the notch between the central and south summits. About three pitches of wet, slippery fourth-class ground lead to a system of ledges, some of them very wide, that runs up to just below the notch, roughly 600 vertical ft above the glacier. From the notch, climb about 400 ft more to the South Peak.

moves.from: Stoppers and slings are enough protection.

beta_new: No detailed move-by-move description of this route has been written down; it is on record as sharing its start with Caravan, which breaks right after the 3rd bolt — Chitlins is presumed to continue more directly.

Ascend the southwest snowfield and scree slopes to reach the summit at 8,459 feet. The route follows the path of least resistance from Fortress-Chiwawa Col, traversing east-northeast aiming for the col, then ascending the final south ridge. Navigate snow or scree to within 100 feet of the summit, then traverse the west side to avoid steep rock sections on the final approach.

A low-fifth-class slab/layback step leads into gully hiking (often holding snow early season) toward the giant chockstone. A 5.7 pitch bypasses the chockstone on the left via blocky terrain and an exposed lieback, historically protected by old pitons, finishing on a delicate slab with sparse bolt protection. Moderate climbing on golden rock with modern bolts, a rightward traverse, and a final loose gully/chimney lead to the summit plateau.

Most parties camp at Boulder Basin and climb Clark as a two-day (sometimes three-day) trip. From camp, drop over Boulder Pass to a bench on Clark's eastern arm, gain the Walrus Glacier, and ascend a moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses and crossing at least one snow-bridge, to a short summit scramble. A glacier-free alternative (the 'Southeast Route') avoids the glacier via a gully out of the south basin but is not the line documented here.

A single, easy blocky low-5th-class pitch up the summit block/'horn,' reached via the standard Snow Lake / Unicorn Creek approach. Considered fun in mixed/early-season conditions and a reasonable solo for confident scramblers, though most parties rope up.

From Reflection Lake, follow the Pinnacle Peak trail up onto the Tatoosh Range crest, then pick up a climbers' path heading west toward Lane Peak; alternatively, approach from Narada Falls, crossing Tatoosh Creek and climbing the gully between Lane and Denman Peaks to the ~5,440 ft Lane-Denman saddle. Technical climbing begins on the east face (~46.7578, -121.7523), alternating exposed scrambling and short protected steps through loose rock, using a sturdy tree roughly 200 ft up as the main anchor, to a small summit perch with views of Rainier, Adams, and St. Helens.

P1 (5.5) climbs about 100 ft up slabby rock on 7 bolts to a chain anchor; P2 (5.10c/d) continues about 80 ft on 9 bolts through the route's crux, pulling a roof near the top. Rated 5.10b overall. It shares the same lichen-covered basalt band as Sidewinder but follows it up and to the left rather than traversing right.
